request: When production goes down, our engineers call the client and it gets worse. They over-explain the technical cause, never say sorry, and can't give a time for the next update. Last month a client in Osaka escalated to our CEO. Ready means: they own it in the first minute, explain impact in plain words and always give a time for the next update.

files.name: client-emails.txt
files.text:
FICTIONAL SAMPLE MATERIAL - made up for the CandiVision Roleplay demo. All names are invented.

From: Head of Operations, Kumo Logistics
To: Account team
Subject: Again??

Our three warehouses stopped for two hours this morning. My team stood idle and trucks left half empty.
This is the second time this month. Last time your engineer spent ten minutes explaining "replication" to me and never told us when it would be fixed.
I do not need the technical details. I need to know what is affected, what you are doing, and when I will hear from you next.
If this happens again I will have to take it to our CEO.

From: Account team
To: Head of Operations, Kumo Logistics
Subject: RE: Again??

We understand. Our on-call engineer will call you now.

files.name: incident-report.txt
files.text:
FICTIONAL SAMPLE MATERIAL - made up for the CandiVision Roleplay demo. Kumo Logistics is not a real company.

Incident report INC-0412 (internal)
Customer: Kumo Logistics (warehouse management platform, Osaka region)
Start: 09:12 local time. Customer impact ended: 11:05.
Impact: warehouse staff could not save new orders. Picking and outbound shipping stopped at three warehouses for about two hours.
Cause: a database schema migration in the morning release locked the orders table. The automatic rollback did not start.
Detection: Kumo's operations team reported it by phone at 09:31. Our monitoring alerted at 09:40.
Fix: release rolled back manually at 10:58. Orders saving again at 11:05.
Next steps: add a lock timeout to migrations; test rollback in staging; send Kumo a written summary within 2 working days.
This is the second incident affecting Kumo this month (the first was a 40-minute login outage on the 3rd).

sources.title: Apology and Restitution: The Psychophysiology of Forgiveness After Accountable Relational Repair Responses
sources.authors: Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet, Lindsey M. Root Luna, Everett L. Worthington, Jo-Ann C. Tsang
sources.summary: Start an outage call by taking clear responsibility, showing empathy for idle teams and stalled shipments, and stating what repair and follow-up will follow, because accountable repair responses increase forgiveness.

sources.title: Breaking bad news with CONSOLE: Toward a framework integrating medical protocols with crisis communication
sources.authors: Kevin Kok-Yew Tan, Augustine Pang, Janelle Xiaoting Kang
sources.summary: Structure bad-news calls with a brief opening that owns the problem, then plain-language impact, actions underway, and a specific next-update time, avoiding jargon like replication or migration internals.

sources.title: Risk and Crisis Communication about Invisible Hazards
sources.authors: Ruth Østgaard Skotnes, Kåre Hansen, Anne Vatland Krøvel
sources.summary: Build trust during uncertain technical events by being honest about what is known and unknown, acknowledging different perceptions of risk, and committing to regular updates rather than waiting for certainty.

sources.title: ANYCaRE: a role-playing game to investigate crisis decision-making and communication challenges in weather-related hazards
sources.authors: Galateia Terti, Isabelle Ruin, Milan Kalaš, Ilona Láng‐Ritter, Arnau Cangròs i Alonso, Tommaso Sabbatini
sources.summary: Use realistic role-play simulations of uncertain, time-pressured incidents to practice deciding what to communicate, when to warn, and how to trigger protective action under pressure.

sources.title: Deliberate Practice and the Acquisition and Maintenance of Expert Performance in Medicine and Related Domains
sources.summary: Train the first-minute ownership and update routine through repeated, focused attempts at the same difficult task with coaching, since expertise grows from sustained deliberate effort not just experience.

sources.title: Formative assessment and self‐regulated learning: a model and seven principles of good feedback practice
sources.summary: Pair each practice call with specific, timely feedback that clarifies the target performance, highlights the gap, and requires the learner to act on it in the next attempt.

sources.title: A model of customer satisfaction with service encounters involving failure and recovery
sources.summary: Customers judge a recovery on three kinds of fairness: what they get back, how quickly and smoothly it is handled, and how they are treated. The best recovery matches the kind and size of the failure; an apology and a fast response matter most when the failure is about the process.

sources.title: An exploration of the structure of effective apologies
sources.summary: Two experiments on which parts of an apology matter. Apologies with more parts were judged more effective. Taking responsibility mattered most, then offering to repair; asking for forgiveness mattered least.

sources.title: PagerDuty Incident Response documentation
sources.summary: An openly published guide to running major incidents. It gives one person the job of communicating with stakeholders, and status updates that say what is affected, what is being done, and when the next update will come.

sources.title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
sources.summary: Expert performance grows through focused practice on specific weak points, with immediate feedback and repetition, at a difficulty just beyond current ability.

sources.title: The power of feedback
sources.summary: A review of feedback in learning. Useful feedback answers where am I going, how am I going, and where to next, and works at the level of the task and the process, not praise of the person.
